The Wealth Tax Officer included a sum of Rs. 1,50,000 estimated as the accrued interest on the assessee 's money lending business. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner and the Appellate Tribunal held that the assessee was entitled to the benefit of the provisions of section 27(1) of the Wealth Tax Act, 1957, and that the Wealth Tax Officer was in law justified in including in the net wealth of the assessee interest due on accrual basis. The High Court in the reference held that the Wealth tax Officer was not in law justified under section 27(i) of the Act, and that as it maintained the books of account in accordance with the cash system of accounting the accrued interest was liable to be included in the wealth tax assessments of the assessee. The High court in the reference under section 27 of the Act held that the net wealth was not to be included as it was not confined to cash. The High Courts in the cases of Commissioner of Wealth Tax, A.P. vs Vysyaraju Badreenarayana Moorthy Raju, , and Commissioner of Wealth tax, A.T.B. and A.T., Andhra Pradesh vs Vysyaaraju Badre, , held that the assets of the assessee were not confined to the cash. The appellants, who were the legal representatives of the deceased plaintiff, filed a suit for a declaration and an injunction to restrain the defendants from dispossessing him from the property in dispute. The suit was dismissed on the ground that the plaintiff was no more in possession of the suit property and, therefore, a suit for declaration and an order of injunction was not maintainable. The defendants, however, contended that the suit was barred by res judicata and that the suit had been barred by resjudicata. The Trial Court upheld the plaintiffs contention and dismissed the suit. The High Court, however, held that the suit filed by the appellants was barred by the principle of res judicata and, therefore the suit was not maintainable and deserved to be dismissed. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The suit was not barred by res Judicata. The suit had been filed in a competent court having jurisdiction at the date of its institution. It would appear unfair to the defendants, and would be for the Trial Court to determine the course of action to be adopted in the light of the guidelines indicated hereinabove. [1020B] 1.2 The plaintiff was not a tenant in respect of the suit land. He was not a trespasser in the property. He was liable to be evicted therefrom. He was, therefore, entitled to the possession of the property. His remedy would, therefore, be to approach the Mamlatdar for decision and after his decision is received by the Civil Court if the issue is held against him. [1021C D] 1.3 The suit was barred under section 58(2) of the Act. [1022D] 2. The suit filed by a person who is a deemed tenant under section 4 of the Act if evicted from the land on or after 1st July, 1962, his remedy under section 8(2) is to approach the authority under the Act for recovery of possession of the land of which he has been dispossessed. In such a situation the remedy may not be the one available in the case of a tenant other than a deemed tenant whose case is not governed by section 8(1) of the Rent Act. But in the case in hand, the suit was filed in a court having jurisdiction in the area in which the suit property was situated. The suit, therefore, was barred by limitation. [1023E F]

The appellant was elected as a trustee by the Sengunatha Brahmins of Manjakollai village in the year 1957. The appellant was elected to the office of a trustee by a member of the Sengunta community. The appellant challenged the election on the ground that the trusteeship of the appellant was not hereditary. The High Court held that the appellant was a hereditary trustee and that the suit was not barred by limitation. The appellant contended that the succession was not hereditary and that the right to the office was not hereditary in the sense that on the death of an existing mahant, his chela does not succeed to the office as a matter of course, because the successor acquires a right only by appointment and the authority to appoint is vested in the assembly of the bairagis and the worshippets. Held, that the appellant is a hereditary trustee within the meaning of the section. The right to the post of trustee in the present case was not hereditary within the meaning Of section 6(9) of the Madras Act 19 of 1951. The appellant 's right to the appointment of the trustee in the instant case was not a hereditary right. The right of the appellant to the office in question was not hereditary, because the office of the appellant being hereditary, the suit was for a fixed period of one year and not for life. The appellant had a right only 'by appointment and the authorities were right in holding that the office of trustee in a hereditary office was not a post abolished. The appellant could not succeed to his office as a hereditary trustee. The appellant is not a hereditary trustee but a hereditary trustee, because his office is a hereditary office. The appellant cannot succeed to his own office. The office of the trustee is for a fixed duration of one year. The appellant, therefore, was a hereditary office within the meaning. of section 6(1) of the Act.

The appellant was convicted under section 52 of the Indian Post Office Act, 1898, and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for one year in each case. The High Court acquitted him of all the offences. The appellant appealed to this Court by special leave. Held, that the prosecution had failed to prove that the appellant had secreted the articles in his possession exclusively or even jointly with his father. The appellant was not in possession of the articles in question and the appellant was not entitled to any benefit of doubt. The appellant had no opportunity to procure the articles from the post office. The appellant could have been convicted under section 51 of the Post Office Act only if he had been in possession of those articles. The appellant 's defence in all these cases was that there were two factions in the Bulandshahr post office and that these articles were planted by the appellant. The appellant, therefore, had an opportunity to procure articles from the Post Office. The appellant did not have any opportunity to procure them from the post offices. The appellant must have been in possession and had the key with him. The appellant would have been in exclusive possession of the keys of the Post office and would have been seriously prejudiced if he had not been in possession. The appellant should have been convicted of the offence of theft. The appellant having been convicted of theft, he could not be convicted of the offences of theft. In the circumstances, the appellant was entitled to the benefit of doubt and the conviction and sentence passed against him. The appeal must be allowed. The appellant is acquitted of all the charges. The appellant has been convicted of all the offenses under section 52 Of the Indian Post Offices Act, 1890, and the sentence passed against the appellant is set aside.

The respondent was convicted by the Special Court established under section 3 of the West Bengal Special Courts Act, 1950, and sentenced to varying terms of imprisonment. The respondent applied to the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution for a writ of certiorari quashing the conviction and the sentence. The High Court quashed the conviction and directed the trial of the respondent and the other accused persons according to law. The respondent 's appeal to the Supreme Court was dismissed. The appellant applied to the Supreme court under article 226 to quash the conviction and sentence on the ground that the Special Court had no jurisdiction to try the case inasmuch as section 5(1) of the Act was not applicable to the case. Held, that the High Court had no power to quash the sentence and the High Court was not justified in quashing the conviction. The High Courts had no jurisdiction under article 226 in the matter of the exercise of their jurisdiction to quash the order of conviction and the High Courts had jurisdiction to quash it. The High ' Court had no inherent power to quash a conviction and the power of the High Court to quash the same was not barred by article 226. The High court had no jurisdiction in the matter. The High, Court had no jurisdic tion to quash the proceedings in the present case. The High. Court had no powers to quash the criminal proceedings in the absence of the accused. The High "Court had no jurisdiction even to try the accused persons. The High" Court had no such jurisdiction. The High ,Court had no inherent powers to quash a criminal proceeding in a court of law. The High Courning of Criminal Procedure Code, 1947, was not a bar to the exercise of the jurisdiction of the High Courts under article 226. It was not necessary for the High Court at that stage to consider the question whether the High Court could exercise its jurisdiction under article 227. The High Power of the High court under article 227 was not a mere power to quash proceedings in a court. The High power of the Supreme Court under article 227 is not only for the High Courts to decide on questions of fact in each case but also for the High courts to decide on the question of fact in every case. The power of the court to quash a sentence is not a mere matter of procedure and it is not necessary for a court to decide on a question of fact. The power to quash is not a matter of mere procedure and it cannot be invoked to quash a court 's own order. The High courts had no jurisdiction when they passed the sentence. It is not necessary that the power should be exercised sparingly and with caution and that the power of quashing should be exercised only when there is a legal bar against the sentence. In the present case the High Court has no inherent power under article 226 and the High court had jurisdiction to interfere with the sentence.

The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The respondent was not liable to pay the sales tax due from his predecessor in title, Purushottam Raju. The respondents, who were the owners of coal mines, were granted coal and coal mining rights in respect of the coal mines. The appellant 's case was that as a result of a letter written by the Inspector of Mines to the respondents, the respondents had encroached upon the coal mines and had rendered the remaining coal of the encroached portion and had rendered it ineffective. The respondents contended that the appellant had encroached upon their coal mines and that the respondents had not taken any steps to remove the coal from the encroached portion. The Subordinate Judge held that the respondents were bound to keep a barrier of 25 feet to the south of the respondent 's working and that the appellant was not entitled to any damages. The Subordinate judge held that the appellant 's action was not bona fide and that the respondent had no knowledge of the appellant ' 's encroachment of their coal mines. On appeal the High Court held that the respondent was not entitled under the Rules to the exemption. Held, that the respondents could not be allowed to take advantage of the fact that the appellant did not take any steps to prevent the respondents from encroaching upon the coal mine and that the coal that was left in the encroached portion was not by any means accessible to the appellant and was wholly unworkable. The respondents had knowledge of the fact of the appellant having encroached upon the appellant '. The respondents were not entitled to the exemption and the appellant was entitled to the benefit of the exemption. The appellant had no knowledge that the respondents 's encroachment was due to the fact that they had encroached upon any portion of their coal mine. The respondents could not, therefore, be allowed to raise the plea of limitation.

The appellant was dismissed from service by the respondent. The appellant challenged the order of dismissal before the High Court. The High Court held that the appellant had intended to take disciplinary action against the respondent and that the order was not a bona fide exercise of the power conferred by r. 18(a) of the Standing Orders. The High court held that the exercise of power was colourable exercise of the powers given to the appellant and therefore its action could not be upheld as a bona fide action. The appellant contended that the order of discharge was not a colourable exercise of power and was not a mala fide exercise of power. Held, that the order passed by the High Court was a colourable exercise and was not in the public interest. The appellant could not rest its case merely on r. 18 (a) and say that having acted under that rule there was nothing more to be said and that the industrial court cannot inquire into the causes that led to the termination of service under r. 18. The appellant cannot rest its case on the ground that the important witnesses, namely, the Engineer, the Secretary and other members of the staff, who were examined by the respondent, were taken by the appellant to the effect that the exercise was colourable and was not bona fide. The appellant was not entitled to rest its case either on the ground of mala fides or on the ground the order was bad. The appellant had no right to rest its claim on the ground, that the important witness, namely, a Engineer, the secretary and other members, who were present in the meeting, had been taken by the respondent to the effect, that the exercise had been bona fide and was not colourable. The appellant failed to satisfy the tribunal when the matter came before it for adjudication that the exercise made by the respondent was bona fide and not colourable.

The appellants, who were the owners of a cinema theatre, filed a suit against the receivers for a declaration that the suit was not maintainable. The receivers were ordered to hand over vacant and peaceful possession of the theatre and to exhibit cinematograph films and to hold "entertainment performances" etc. The receivers filed a suit for a declaration and injunction against the receivers. The receivers, on the other hand, were restrained from interfering directly or indirectly with the rights of the receivers. On appeal the receivers were directed to hand over the vacant and peaceful pos session of the theatre to the receivers. In the meantime, the receivers filed a petition for a declaration of their rights and for a declaration to the effect that the suit had been instituted by the receivers and that the receivers had no right to exhibit the suit. The receivers also claimed that the receivers were bound and liable to allow the receivers to exercise their rights in the theatre. The receivers contended that the receivers could not be directed to handover the vacant and vacant possession of the cinema theatre and to hold the same. The receivers appealed to the High Court. The High Court held that the receivers having been directed to hand back the vacant and live possession of the Theatre, the receivers could be restrained from interfering with the rights and privileges of the receivers and the receivers. Held, that the receivers, in the absence of a consent decree, could not be restrained from exercising their rights in a suit for declaration of their right to exhibit a cinema theatre and the receivers could only be restrained from taking any action in the suit. Held, further, that the receiver could not be permitted to interfere with the rights or privileges of the receiver and the receivers were not bound to allow the receiver to exercise their right of exhibit a cinema film and to hold a cinema theatre. The receiver could not, therefore, be restrained from proceeding with the suit.

The appellant, a company, entered into an agreement with the respondents, an award for payment of wages to its employees. The appellant contended that the respondents were not entitled to the benefits of the Act, and that the respondents had no right to claim wages under the Act. Held, that the appellant had no right, under the Act, to claim wages as defined by section 2(vi) of the Act. The appellant had paid the respondents the minimum wages fixed by the award in accordance with the provisions of section 2(v) of the . The respondents were not liable to pay wages under the provisions of that Act. The respondents were entitled to the same. The appellant was not entitled to claim wages for the period of the award. The respondents had no option to pay wages to the appellant under the Act before it was amended. The amendment made by the Amending Ordinance of 1958, which was a part of the award, was not retrospective in operation. The appellant could not claim wages under section 2(i) of the 1948 Act. The award was made by an Industrial Tribunal. The appellant 's claim was barred by limitation. The appellant company was incorporated in January, 1946 as a Private Limited Company to take over the business of the partnership firm of the Shaw Wallace and Co., which had been run by the respondent company. The age of retirement of the appellant workmen was raised to 60 and the Tribunal held that the age of retirement should be 58 but the Tribunal held in favour of the appellant. The Tribunal held that it was not possible to fix the retirement age of the appellant employees at 60 and that the age should be 58 and that the appellant should be fixed at 60. The Tribunal also held that the retirement age should be raised to 60 but the Tribunal directed that the age for retirement should be raised at 60 and not the age of superannuation. The appellant contended that the age fixed by the Tribunal was not correct and that the Tribunal had not taken into consideration the fact that the age was fixed at 60 and the age fixed was not unreasonable. Held, that the Tribunal was right in holding that the age could not be fixed at 55 and that the tribunal had not taken any other view of the matter. The Tribunal had not considered the question whether it should be fixed on the basis of the age of the employees of the respondent company or whether it should have fixed the retirement age at 60. It was not correct to say that the age had to be raised to 58 and that it was open to the Tribunal to consider the question whether the age of compulsory retirement should be fixed in the light of the decision of this Court in the case of the Bombay region. The Tribunal was right. The Tribunal has not considered the evidence on record and has come to the conclusion that the age has to be raised at 55. The Tribunal 's conclusion that the retirement of the respondent workmen should be raised before the Tribunal was correct. The Tribunal, therefore, was right in taking the view that the age at 55 should be raised and that the retirement should be made on the basis that the age is raised to 60. The fact that in the Bombay region at least there is a general agree ment that the age will be raised to 55 and that in the present case the age of retire should be raised. The Tribunal therefore had to consider the matter afresh and decide the question whether in the circumstances of the case the age should not be raised to the age of 60.

The company could not, therefore, be said to have been carrying on the business of the company in the name and style of "M/s. Humphreys and Glascow Ltd. " within the meaning o section 2(2) of the Act. [319 E] (2) The company could be said to carry on business in its name and could not be held to be a "public Company" within the definition. [319 D] (3) The company had been doing business in the names of the companies and had been carrying out the necessary repairs at their cost. The company did not carry on the business in the company. [319 C] (4) The company did carry on business as a private company. The directors of the company were not members of the company, but were members of the public. The directors were not members. The appellant was detained under the impugned order of detention on the 8th June 1955, and was in detention for more than three years. The grounds of detention were vague. The appellant, a manufacturer of gold, was granted a license to sell gold to the respondents. The license was granted to the respondents on the security of certain articles, ornament or both in the same premises in which he carried on business as a money lender or banker on the security. The license granted to the appellant was renewed for a period of three years. The licence was renewed for three years. In the meantime the licence was granted to him. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of section 28 of the Gold Control Act, 1968. The High Court held that the appellant was not entitled to the license. The High court held that the license was valid and the appellant was entitled to the grant of the license. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the High Court was wrong in holding that the license granted to a dealer was valid and that the appellant could not be granted the license. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: The High Court was right in holding that section 28 of Gold Control Act 1968 was invalid. The High Courts have upheld the validity of the section. The High 'Court was therefore right in holding the appellant was bound to grant the license. [957 B C] The High Court 's view that the appellant had not been able to establish that the license had been granted by the Administrator in the interest of the public or that the appellant did not have the necessary financial or professional interest in the business of the appellant, was not correct. [958 E] The appellant was not a dealer in gold. He was prevented only from carrying on business as money lender or Banker on the Security of any article, ornament, or both. Therefore, the license granted by the appellant was valid. [959 B C] In the instant case the appellant was a dealer in the gold. He had been prevented only from carry on business as cash lender or bankers on the security, of any article ornament or either of them. The appellant was prevented only by the Administrator from carrying on the business as a cash lender or Bankers on the Security. The appellant had been prevented from carrying on his business as money lending or banker. The appellant could not have been prevented only by a few months ' time. [960 E F] The appellant had not shown that he was not a person in the business or trade of the appellant. The appellant did not show that he was a person in business or trade. The appellant, therefore, was not entitled for the license.[960 E] The High court was right in its view that the license did not confer any arbitrary, uncanalised power on the Administrator to grant or renew a license to a dealer. [961 F] The High Courts were therefore not justified in holding that sec. 28 of the Act was invalid. [962 E] The Bombay High Court in Ramanlal Purshottamdas Chokshi vs Union of India & Ors. , held that the licence granted to the respondent was valid and was valid. The High. Court was therefore right. [963 F]

The appellants were not liable to prosecution for contravention of section 14 of Act. The Act did not authorise the levy of a penalty on the appellants. The appellants had no locus standi to the proceedings. The Act, therefore, did not apply, and the provisions of section 14 were not applicable to them. The appellants could not be prosecuted for contraventions of section 14. The Act does not apply to transactions in which trade allowance is made. The Act only applies to transactions in respect of commercial crops. The deduction may be out of the commodity or out of the price. The payment of the price or commodity agreed to be paid or transferred, it would be a trade allowance. The appellants, therefore, were not liable for the contravention of section 15 of the Act and were liable to be prosecuted for the contravention. The appellants did not have any locus standi to maintain the appeals. The appellants are not liable to be convicted for contraventions. The Act is not a law relating to trade allowance. It is not a trade allowance, but a trade allowance and is not a tax on the sale price of goods. The appellants cannot be prosecuted for breach of the provisions. The Act merely provides for the levy of penalty on the sale of goods. If the payment is de hors the terms of the transaction but made towards consideration for the use of the premises or for the services rendered, it would not be a sale in the course of trade. The appellants therefore were not liable.

The appellants who were displaced persons from West Pakistan were granted quasi permanent allotment of the village panchayats in 1949 and the land allotted to them in substitution of the lands at evacuees was given quasi permanent allotment in another village. The appellants filed a revision application before the Custodian General, Evacuee Property, but the Additional Custodian for the State of Punjab cancelled the allotment of the lands in favour of the appellants. The Additional Custodian, however, dismissed the revision application on the ground that the appellants were not entitled to allotment of suburban land. The appellants preferred an appeal to the Custodian General. The Custodian General, however, allowed the appeal on the ground of delay and cancelled the allotment. The appellants appealed to the Custodian, who dismissed the appeal on merits. The Custodian, however dismissed the revision on the ground, inter alia, that the appellants had no locus standi to file the revision application. The appellants then filed a revision petition before the Custodian, which was dismissed. The appellants came to this Court by special leave. Held, that the Custodian General was right in holding that the appellants could not make out a new case at this stage of argument. The appellants were not precluded from challenging the order of cancellation of the allotment in their favour by the Custodian General on the ground inter alia that the order of the Custodian was not a transfer of the property of the appellants to the manager and therefore could not be said to be an order of cancellation. The order of the Additional Custodian was not an order of the Deputy Custodian. The order was not a mere order of cancellation but was a mere order by the Custodian. The Custodian was not competent to cancel the allotment in favour of any one else. The order did not amount to a transfer of property of the appellant to the manager. The order could not be challenged on the ground only that it was an order of transfer of property. The order, however, did not amount either to a transfer or to a transfer. The order merely stated that the order was to be made by the Custodian and not to a transfer and it was not a case of cancellation of an allotment. The order does not amount to an order of a transfer of land. The order is not a mere an order of allotment but a mere order for the purpose of making an order of confirmation. The order must be a mere order or an order of an allotment and not a mere one. The order in the present case was not a sale of land but a transfer of a property in the compensation pool. The order made by the Additional Custodian on the ground merely stated that he was not a party to the proceedings before the Custodian. Held, further, that the order did not create any right in the appellants to make the allotment of land. Held, also, that the orders of the Additional Director of Evacuee Property, Evacuee Property and the Additional Custodian were not final and could not be questioned in the proceedings before him. The order passed by the Additional Director was not a final order of the evacuee property and was not a nullity.

The Andhra Pradesh Government issued a notification dated October 29, 1979, amending the Fundamental Rules, and the Andhra Pradesh Government Order dated October 29. 1979, which provided that the age of retirement of all Government employees, whether ministerial or non ministerial, but not belonging to the last Grade Service, who had already attained the age of 55 years was to retire from service with effect from February 28, 1983. The petitioners, who were Government servants, challenged the validity of the said order and the notifications on the ground that they had become necessary to provide greater employment opportunities to the youths. The High Court dismissed the petitions. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the proviso to Article 309 was not a legislative power and that the amendment of the Fundamental Rules was not a legislation within the legislative field. Dismissing the petitions, ^ HELD: 1. The proviso to Article 162 of the Constitution is a legislative power. The proviso is of a legislative character and is to be distinguished from an ordinary rule making power. The power to legislate is of a judicial character and is not to be equated with an ordinary rule. The power of the legislature to amend the Fundamental Rules is of a Parliamentary or State character and is subject to the legislative power of the State. The proviso does not confer any power on the legislature to alter the conditions of service of the employees of the State Government. The proviso merely confers power on the State Government to alter the terms of service of its employees. The proviso only confers power on Government to alter conditions of service. The proviso cannot be amended retrospectively so as to take away rights which had already accrued to the youth employees. [648 G H] 2. The proviso which conferred a benefit upon Government servants by protecting their conditions of service cannot be amended so as to bring the Fundamental Rules into force retrospectively. The proviso, therefore, cannot be amended subsequently so as to remove the rigour of the proviso. [649 B] 3. The proviso was a legislative power, and was to be construed as a legislative power within the legislative fields. The proviso did not confer any right on the Government servant to claim the benefit of the proviso to article 309. The proviso could not be amended retrospectively. [651 C] 4. The proviso has no application to the case of the petitioners. The proviso in the instant case, therefore, is not a legislative act. [652 E] 5. The proviso must be read as a legislative act and it includes the power to legislate retrospectively. [752 E]

The property in question was leased to the appellant under two lease deeds in favour of M/s India Automobiles. The first lease was dated 22.9.1947 and related to Door No. 2 (Item No. 1 in Schedule A to the plaint) covered an area of 4 grounds and 1515 sq. It belonged to several co owners. The rent was Rs. 150 per month. On 30.7.1953, the LIC moved two applications (being HRC Nos. 3310 and 3311 of 1965) in the court of the Rent Controller for fixation of a "fair rent" for each of the premises. The Rent Controller, on the basis of the rent fixed under the lease deed, held that the lease was a statutory lease and that the superstructure had been built by them. The appellant filed objections to the application. The Rent Control Tribunal held that the rent was payable by the appellant and that the building was let out to the respondent. The appellant preferred an appeal to the Rent Control Tribunal. The Tribunal held that there was a relationship of landlord and tenant between the parties and that the lease deed was a statutory tenancy and that the appellant was entitled to relief under the Madras Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1950. The High Court, in appeal, held that there were two different tenancies and that the question of the relationship of landlord & tenant was one of fact and that the respondent was entitled to the relief of eviction under the Madras Act. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court was wrong in holding that the Rent Controller had no jurisdiction to decide the question of title and that the Rent Control Act did not provide for a machinery for recovery of the amount. HELD: The High Court was right in holding that there was no relationship of landlord, tenant and tenant between both the parties. [557E] The Rent Control Act does not provide for any machinery for recovery by the landlord of rent from the tenant. The Rent Act does not contemplate any machinery for the recovery of the rent from the landlord. The Rent controller has to deal with the matter in a fair and just manner. The Rent control Act does not make a distinction between a landlord and tenant and the Rent Controller has to deal in a fair manner. The Act does not envisage any machinery for recovering the rent from a tenant. The Act contemplates a machinery for the eviction of a tenant from the tenant and the tenant is entitled to recover the rent from him. The Act also contemplates a machinery to recover the amount from the tenant only by recourse to a civil court. This is also made clear by the provisions relating to eviction. [549F G]

The Tribunal held that the cost of the container should be included in the assessable value of the goods for the purpose Of the excise duty. The Tribunal, however, held that in the absence of any evidence to show that the cost was not includible in the assessable price of the goods, the value of such packing should be included. The cost is to be included. [981G H] 4. The cost in the instant case, is to be excluded from the assessable value. [989G H]

The State Government appointed a Pay Rationalisation Committee with wide ranging reference. The Committee recommended for them a pay scale slightly lower than that of Section Officers. The Committee submitted its report in which the Committee recommended that the pay scale of Rs. 160 320 as recommended by the Committee was not comparable with that of Section Officer. The Committee, however, recommended that the post of Section Officer be placed in the scale of Rs 160 320 as against the pay scale Rs. 200 450. The Committee also recommended that the posts of Section Officers be placed in scale of Rs 200 450. On the basis of the recommendations of the Committee, the Committee recommended the pay scale for Section Officers. On the recommendations of a Committee, the Government appointed the Pay Commission as a Selection Committee. The Committee was asked to consider the duties and responsibilities of different categories of posts. The Committee suggested that the pay scales of Section Officers should be fixed on the basis of their seniority cum merit and that the merit will be evaluated by a Selection Committee consisting of three members. The Committee considered the duties and responsibility of the Section Officers and recommended that the Section Officers should also be given the same pay scale. The Committee accordingly recommended that the Sub Section Officers should at least be put at par with Section Officers if not on higher scale. The High Court accepted the recommendation of the Committee and directed that the Section officers should be put at the same scale of pay as Section Officers. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High Court was in error in holding that the Section Officer was discriminated against in the matter of pay scales of Rs.1600 2950 to Section Officers. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Courts have overlooked the criterion provided under the Rules. The merit will depend on the seniority cum merit or merit cum seniority. The differentiation so made in the same cadre will not amount to discrimination. [292G] 2. The classification based on experience is a reasonable classification. It has a rational nexus with the object sought to be achieved. [292A] 3. The classification is a reasonable one. It has, therefore, a rational nexus to the object sought for. [292C] 4. The classification made under the Rules, therefore, cannot be said to be violative of the right to have equal pay for equal work. [292D] 5. The classification has a rational relation to the object to be achieved, namely, to provide equal pay for unequal work. The differentiation is a reasonable differentia. It has an rational nexus with that object. [292E]

The appellant Companies were the owners of certain lands in the State of Madhya Pradesh. The State Government issued a notification under section 55 of the Madhya Pradesh Nagar Tatha Gram Nivesh Adhiniyam, 1973, for the purpose of making provision for the development and use of land. The appellant Companies were required to pay a sum of Rs. 1,00,000 to the Housing Commissioner of the State. The appellant companies were required to make provision for the compulsory acquisition of land required for the purpose. The appellant company filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the notification. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant companies that the notification was invalid because the notification was issued under section 55 and was not in accordance with the provisions of the Act of 1957. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The notification was invalid. The notification was valid. [627F] (2) The notification did not result in invalidation of every State legislation relating to mines and minerals. The notification did no purport to be invalid. The State Legislature had no competence to pass the impugned Act by reason of Entry 52, List I read with Entry 24, List II. The notification, therefore, was invalid. [628G] (3) The notification in question was invalid. It was not in the public interest that the State Government should have exercised its power of taxation under Entry 24, list II. [629A] (4) The notification, in fact, did not result into invalidation of every state legislation relating to the mines and minerals, and was therefore within the competence of the State Legislature. [631B] (5) The notification merely stated that the State Legislature had the competence to enact the impugned Act. [632C] (6) The notification had no application to the facts of the case. [633D] (7) The notification could not be said to be invalid merely because the notification did not contain any provision for the acquisition of land. [634D] (8) The notification issued under section 54 of the Act was invalid. There was no question of the notification being invalid. [630G] (8)(a) The notification under section 54 was invalid. In the instant case, the notification was valid and the notification was not in conformity with the provisions contained in the Act of the 1957 Act. [630A] (b) The notification dated June 24, 1976 was invalid.

The appellant, who was the lessee of a minor, was granted a lease of the lands in dispute by the Rajah for a period of 20 years commencing from February 1, 1947, and ending on November 30, 1947. On the expiry of the fifth year, the Rajah granted a lease to the appellant for a period exceeding the period of the lease. On December 10, 1947 the appellant applied to the Collector for confirmation of the lease and the Collector passed an order on December 10, 1950, cancelling the lease. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the order of the Collector on the ground that the order of cancellation was invalid as it was passed without the previous sanction of the Government. The High Court dismissed the petition. On appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The order of the Government cancelling the lease was invalid as the Government had no power to cancel the lease. [561 E] (ii) The Government must have exercised its power under the second proviso to section 20(1) of the Abolition Act. The second proviso to the section does not apply to the case of the appellant. The second Proviso does not apply in the present case. The Government must do something to avoid them. There is no warrant for saying that the avoidance must be under the terms of the third proviso. If the third proviso at all applied to rights created after July 1, 1945, then the second proviso would be otiose and need not have been enacted at all. [562 E F] (iii) The second proviso does not apply where the Government had not exercised its power earlier under the second Proviso. The second and the third proviso deal with the termination of rights created after the expiry of two months notice. The second is a self contained proviso and the aid of the third Proviso would be wholly uncalled for. [563 E]
